summary: A 1970 note on a way for protocols to be proffered officially, by four authors. It is updated by RFC 57.

plainLanguage.summary: This 1970 note offers a first common set of rules for how one computer opens a conversation with another, controls how much data it may send, and ends the conversation. The authors published it for comment before making it official.

subtitle: The June 1970 draft of the first official host-to-host protocol of the early ARPA network, offered for comment.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the early network needed one agreed way to open connections, regulate how much data flows over them, and close them again.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts exchange short control commands such as STR, RTS, CLS and ALL on control link 1; the receiver tells the sender how much buffer space is available, and the sender never sends more text than that.
tldr.outcome: The authors hoped it would become the initial official protocol and invited criticism until July 13, 1970. It was updated by RFC 57.

today: RFC 54 is a 1970 draft whose status is recorded as Unknown, and it was updated by RFC 57. The text shows an early stage of the host-to-host protocol, not a current specification.

sections.title: A Protocol Offered for Comment
sections.content:
RFC 54, by Steve Crocker, Jon Postel, John Newkirk and Mike Kraley, submits a protocol for criticism and comment, as advertised in NWG/RFC 53. The authors intend it to become the initial official protocol and invite criticism until July 13, 1970. After that date a decision would be made whether to adopt it, or a slight variation, or to redesign it.

It covers only network-wide issues, which the authors define as message formats and restrictions on message content. Writing a Network Control Program (NCP) and choosing system calls are strictly local matters. A prototypical NCP is described in RFC 55.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors are saying: here are our proposed rules, tell us what is wrong with them before we make them official. The single network-wide subject is the shape of messages and what they may contain.

sections.title: Connections, Sockets and Links
sections.content:
A connection is a simplex communication path, intended to run between two processes. The protocol provides for establishing connections, regulating flow over them, and terminating them, plus ancillary functions such as simulated interrupt pulses and echoing test messages.

Connections are named by a pair of sockets, described in the discussion as 40-bit names known throughout the network; the command formats later give my socket and your socket as 32-bit fields made of a 24-bit user number and an 8-bit AEN. Sockets are polarized: even-numbered ones are receive sockets and odd-numbered ones are send sockets, and one of each is required.

Each connection is also assigned a unique link, chosen by the receiver. Link 1 between each pair of hosts is the control link, link zero is reserved for intra-network use, links 32 to 255 are reserved for experiment and expansion, and so only links 2 through 31 are available for regular use.
sections.plainLanguage: A connection is a one-way path between two programs. Each end has a numbered socket, and a small number called a link keeps one connection's traffic apart from another's.

sections.title: Flow Control with Allocations
sections.content:
The one substantive change from the protocol already agreed is a new flow control scheme. The receiving host allocates buffer space for each connection and tells the sending host how much space, in bits, is available. The sending host keeps a counter per connection, initializes it to zero, raises it by control commands from the receiver, and lowers it by the text length of each message sent. It may not send more text than the counter holds, so the counter never goes below zero.

The command ALL <link> <space> carries the allocation and is sent only from the receiving host to the sending host. The RFC admits an obvious limitation: the receiver cannot rely on average buffer usage, since the worst case is always assumed. Adaptive allocation is judged feasible but is left for later. Separately, a sender is held by the local IMP from sending another message over a connection until the RFNM for the previous message arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver tells the sender how much data it has room for, and the sender keeps a running count of the space left. When the count is exhausted the sender waits for a new allocation before sending more.

sections.title: Control Commands
sections.content:
A regular message consists of a 32-bit leader, marking, text and padding. A regular message sent over the control link (link 1) is a control message, and its text is a whole number of control commands. Every control command code is 8 bits long.

To establish a connection, the prospective sender sends STR and the prospective receiver sends RTS, which also carries the link field. A matching pair, where each side's my socket equals the other's your socket, establishes the connection. CLS terminates it, and each side must send and receive one before the sockets are free again. INR and INS carry interrupts, ECO and ERP form a simple echo test, NOP does nothing, and ERR reports an apparent error. The text defines no specific error list, and says hosts should log ERR commands.
sections.plainLanguage: Each command is a short message identified by a number: one asks to open a connection, one frees the space, one says how much more may be sent. The RFC lists ten such codes, from NOP at zero to ERR at nine.

items.label: NOP
items.desc: No operation; coded as zero to simplify message construction.

items.label: RTS
items.desc: Request connection, receiver to sender; carries a link field.

items.label: ALL
items.desc: Allocate buffer space for a link.

items.label: INR
items.desc: Interrupt sent by the receiving process.

items.label: INS
items.desc: Interrupt sent by the sending process.
